refutation.note: Read all 16 after.jsonl items (result-60d899, -eb9211, -6de887, -6d422d, -36e8cd, -0018d3, -afc423, knowledge-13cff3, -9d979a, -d68d37, -ffebc2, -c57b51, -5da8a9, plus three UI items), the board's 60 newest result/knowledge items, and the before items on the checkpoints (knowledge-9c5052, -87618d, -0b450e, -c1fe13, -b15a21, -8a31ad, result-7968b8, -533123, -e870a1). None reports T 0.6 cap hits for steps 100, 400 or 2,800 that go against the theory. The stored rows support the predicted shape: on plain MATH-500 the base has 65 cap hits, step 100 has 103, step 400 has 98 and step 2,800 has about 16 (464 right, 484 finished). On the clean 328 the base has 137 and step 400 has 160. Two weak tensions. (a) Step 100 has slightly more cap hits than step 400, and its neuron changes sit at the noise floor (knowledge-9c5052). So the rise is already at its full size by step 100, while the theory's point predictions (0.03 at step 100, 0.06 at step 400) assumed it keeps growing through step 400. (b) knowledge-13cff3 (after the cutoff): in the cued base at T 0.6, loop rule A flags 70 of 98 cap hits (71 %). That is close to step 400's 80 % (78 of 98), so the loop share of cap hits does not show any extra sharpening at step 400. Neither contradicts the theory outright.

wins_judgement: The gains are 2.89, 3.0 and 3.0 nats on p1-p3 (the cap-hit difference against the base at step 100, step 400 plain, and step 400 on the hard set) and 0.97 on p5. All come from one claim: cap hits at T 0.6 rise before they fall. Both readers expected a fall in all three (centres -0.025 to -0.12), so the rise-then-fall shape earned these gains. The entropy and top-p-lock part of the mechanism did not: no test measures entropy or the lock (the rows store mean_logprob, which could have tested it). A reader without the mechanism could have predicted a rise from the 3.0 numbers on the board (29.1 % vs 17.8 % cap hits, knowledge-b15a21) plus the much longer RL answers (median 2,856 vs 609 tokens, knowledge-0b450e). P5 (80 % of step-400 cap hits are loops) sits in the high end of the readers' intervals. Base cap hits are about 71 % loops (knowledge-13cff3), so p5 says that most cap hits are loops, not that sharpening adds loops. P4 (accuracy on finished answers) could not be computed: math_verify is missing. So the accuracy half of phase 1 is untested. I read p2.py. It implements the recipe exactly: sample == 0, first row per problem_index, intersection S, cap_hit with the finish_reason fallback, and the difference over |S| (500 problems, 98 vs 65 cap hits).
rival: The stated rival (truncation negatives act from the first steps, so cap hits fall monotonically) is refuted by p1-p3, where all three differences are positive (+0.076, +0.066, +0.070). It is also refuted by p5, since step-400 cap hits are mostly rule-A loops and not long deliberation that never loops. That rival is a straw man, though. The stronger rival nobody tested is length growth: early RL makes the model deliberate longer (more 'Wait' bursts) before it learns to stop, so more answers reach the cap and loop under T 0.6, with no entropy or lock mechanism needed. It predicts the same p1-p3 and p5 numbers. Three measurements would separate the two: (i) the per-token entropy or mean_logprob of finished answers at step 100/400 against the base (the theory says sharper, length growth says no change needed); (ii) the cap-hit difference at step 400 under T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 (the theory says it vanishes, because pure sampling never locks; length growth says it stays); (iii) the finished-answer length distribution at step 100/400. The held-out prediction 6 (T 1.0 at step 400) partly tests (ii), but it was not run.

novelty.nearest: Tricks or Traps (2508.08221) Sec 4.4.1 and Fig. 15: with a 20k limit, overlong samples are dominated by repetitive outputs that never stop, and the share of these grows during RL. In their reading, filtering (masking) overlong samples lowers that share. Also 2512.12895 (looping is a low-temperature effect) and 2610.24715 (top-p locks loops). The rise-then-fall of intrinsic-reward RLVR (2603.08660) is about accuracy, not loops.
novelty.difference: No paper found describes a loop rate that rises and then falls across checkpoints of one RL run, with a sharper early policy pushing top-p sampling at low temperature into loops and truncation negatives later removing them. 2508.08221 even reports that masking truncations, not penalising them, lowered the repetitive share (on aligned Qwen3-8B), which goes against the theory's phase-2 reading.

import_carries_gain.which: No import carries a winning claim. The gains come from cap hits at steps 100/400 compared with the base, which no paper measures. 2505.22617 (early entropy drop) and 2610.24715 (top-p lock) motivate the rise, but the tests check neither entropy nor locking. 2610.30882 (3.0 has more cap hits than its base) is the closest support for a rise, but it concerns a final checkpoint of another release. 2508.08221 is misread: its Fig. 15 says overlong filtering lowered the repetitive share, so it does not support 'penalising truncations trains loops out'.

verdict: weak: the rise-then-fall of T 0.6 cap hits (base 65 -> step 100 103 / step 400 98 -> step 2,800 about 16) is real and beat both readers, but the theory's mechanism (entropy collapse pushing sampling past top-p's lock threshold) was never tested, an untested length-growth rival explains the same numbers, the accuracy prediction could not be computed, and one import is misread.
